claims.text: The initial alloy is a cast multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy with lamellar alpha and beta phases.
The initial alloy has an average grain size of approximately 5 micrometers.
The initial alloy possesses a dewetted high-temperature passive oxide film.
Sliding wear removes the high-temperature passive oxide preferentially at lamellar phase boundaries.
Oxide removal exposes anodic eutectic phases to localized microgalvanic attack.
The alpha and beta eutectic phases have a galvanic potential difference relevant to localized corrosion.
Freshly exposed alpha/beta interfaces act as microanodes.
Rapid localized pitting occurs at the exposed phase interfaces.
Localized corrosion undermines or embrittles phase interfaces and thereby increases removal by wear.
Corrosion defects concentrate mechanical stress and accelerate subsequent oxide breakdown.
The coupled feedback between oxide removal, localized corrosion, and interface weakening produces synergistic degradation.
Combined wear-corrosion mass loss will exceed the sum of wear-only and corrosion-only mass losses.
The wear contribution during the combined test will exceed wear-only mass loss.
Corrosion current during combined wear-corrosion will exceed that during static corrosion-only exposure.
Passive-film integrity and regrowth kinetics at alpha/beta boundaries mediate the degradation response.
The proposed mechanism is valid over 1–5 wt% NaCl, 250–350 degrees Celsius, sliding speeds of 10–20 cm/s, loads of 5–15 N, oxygen partial pressures of at least 0.05 atm, and up to 100000 cycles.
A homogenized single-phase alloy of the same overall composition provides a matched microstructural baseline.
Corrosion attack should be preferentially localized at phase boundaries rather than uniformly distributed.

contradictions.description: The combined exposure is defined as 3.5 wt% NaCl aqueous vapor, whereas the corrosion-only arm is described as immersion. These are not identical environmental conditions and can produce different transport, wetting, and electrochemical behavior.

The intervention specifies electrochemical operation at open-circuit potential, while chronoamperometry ordinarily requires an imposed potential and measures current under potentiostatic control. The intended electrochemical control and current measurement mode are therefore inconsistent or insufficiently defined.
